teaser: End an email reply with the state of the thread for this reader, not the quoted wall: decided, open, next, who is on copy, with links to the record.
core_idea: The quoted wall under a reply is redundant and occupies the space where a reader asks what they need to know; replace it with a short, reader-specific state of the thread, derived from the record and linking back to it, drafted by the agent team's drafts role from typed blocks and reviewed by a person, and run as an experiment rather than a format.

nodes.label: The quoted wall is redundant
nodes.summary: Every reply ships the whole thread to a reader who already has it, and the clients hide it on arrival behind a trimmed-content link.

nodes.label: The reader's questions
nodes.summary: Where are we, what was decided, what is open and whose, what happens next and do I act, who is on this thread now; the wall holds the material and answers none of them.

nodes.label: End with the state of the thread
nodes.summary: Decided, open, next, on copy, sources: a hundred words written for this reader, with links to the messages condensed, which stay in the thread as the record.

nodes.label: Written for one reader
nodes.summary: The same thread condenses differently for the counterparty, the newcomer and the colleague who read everything; the question is what this person needs now.

nodes.label: Who is on copy is part of the state
nodes.summary: Who joined, who left, which participants are agents: facts every newcomer needs that no quoted wall carries.

nodes.label: Derived, not the record
nodes.summary: The tail points back at the thread instead of repeating it; if the tail is wrong the record underneath is not, and the reader can check in one tap.

nodes.label: Netiquette, BLUF, Minto, TL;DR, ADRs
nodes.summary: RFC 1855 asked for a summary instead of the full quote in 1995; the Army's bottom line up front; the Pyramid Principle; decision records with a Status line.

nodes.label: Reader-side AI summaries
nodes.summary: Superhuman, Shortwave, Copilot in Outlook, Apple Mail and Gmail now compute a summary at the top of a thread for the reader, privately and regenerated each time.

nodes.label: Sender's statement versus reader's view
nodes.summary: The client summary belongs to one reader and nobody stands behind it; the tail is reviewed, shared with everyone on copy, in the record, and can be argued with.

nodes.label: The drafts role writes it
nodes.summary: From the typed blocks the inbox role already captures, for a chosen reader, with message ids cited and a hash logged; the person edits and sends; the inbox role records what went out.

nodes.label: Personal, so configurable
nodes.summary: Five rows, one line, or the wall back: the reader's preference is a row in their folder in the CRM; text first, richer forms are variants.

nodes.label: An experiment, not a format
nodes.summary: Four variants rotated by thread for a month on one person's correspondence, with measurements the record can take and the results published either way.

nodes.label: What would make this wrong
nodes.summary: Readers scrolling to the quotes anyway, condensations corrected in more than a few replies in ten, clients mangling the rows.

nodes.label: What does not exist yet
nodes.summary: The drafts role writing tails automatically, the preference row, the templates, the measurement report, the month of data and the follow-up.

quotes.text: The wall is shipped with every message and hidden on arrival, which is the clearest possible sign that it is the wrong thing to ship.
quotes.why: The observation the proposal starts from.

quotes.text: The client's summary says what the thread looks like from here; the tail says what the sender believes it is.
quotes.why: How the proposal differs from the AI summaries mail clients already compute.
